strengths: Novel and conceptually clean idea: decomposing each LoRA rank-r update into r rank-one key-value pairs and letting each rank's A row (key) act as its own router for its B column (value) removes the need for a separate router, saving parameters and simplifying the architecture. The framing via linear associative memory is well-developed and motivates the design.

Broad and thorough empirical evaluation across modalities and models: CLIP on MTIL and X-TAIL, T5-large and LLaMA2-7B on standard and 15-task LM streams under multiple orderings, plus a generalization/forgetting study on Llama-3.1-8B with HumanEval and MMLU. MoRA is consistently best or near-best across these settings.

Demonstrated parameter efficiency: Table 10 and Table 15 show MoRA activates fewer parameters per task than MoE-LoRA/MoE-Adapter while matching a rank-32 LoRA on code generation with roughly one-third of the activated parameters.

The rank-activation visualizations (Figs. 3, 5, 6) provide concrete evidence for rank specialization, stable reuse across tasks, and reduced interference, which is more convincing than aggregate accuracy alone.

Reasonable reproducibility details (datasets, prompts, hyperparameters, rank budgets, temperatures, thresholds) and an honest ablation that reports the (near-tied) comparison between self-activation and a learned rank-level router rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The headline gains are marginal. Against the strongest baselines, improvements are often within noise (e.g., X-TAIL Average 72.7 vs CoDyRA 71.3, Transfer 63.3 vs 63.2; MTIL Average 73.9 vs 73.3; LM Table 3 77.6 vs LB-CL 76.7; 15-task Table 8 69.72 vs 69.2; MMLU 63.70 vs 63.59). The paper's language of 'substantial' improvement overstates the evidence.

The central claim that self-activation is preferable to a learned router is weakly supported. Table 4 shows Non-self-activation (65.97/69.76 on Average/Last) is essentially tied with Self-activation (65.94/69.85); the benefit is mainly parameter savings, not accuracy, yet the narrative implies routing quality is improved.

The ablation indicates most of the gain comes from temperature (sharpness) scaling alone (66.52->71.15 Average, 70.62->79.62 Last when adding tau), so the contribution of the rank-one decomposition itself is not isolated from a single well-tuned hyperparameter. There is no direct ablation of the decomposition against standard LoRA in the same CL setup.

The three motivating 'challenges' (interference, redundancy, routing ambiguity) are asserted rather than empirically quantified; no measurement is provided to show that these are the actual failure modes of MoE-LoRA baselines.

Computational cost of the method is under-reported: computing scores over all accumulated ranks (r_t grows with T) per token is a scaling concern that is not analyzed, and the test-time thresholding adds an inference-time hyperparameter whose sensitivity (Fig. 4c) is only lightly explored.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: reference typos (e.g., 'Grattafori' for Grattafiori, 'Douvitskiy' for Dosovitskiy), inconsistent table headers (e.g., 'Front'/'OxfordPnt' in Table 13), and a confusing discrepancy between the CLIP Zero-shot Average (58.5) and the Transfer-section Zero-shot value (62.4) that is not explained in the table.

The MMLU/HumanEval differences used to argue for preserved generalization are small (often sub-point), and no variance/statistical testing is provided for these specific claims (variance is only reported for the CLIP X-TAIL runs in Table 13).

strengths: The core idea—decomposing each rank-r LoRA update into r rank-one components and treating each as an independently routable expert via the key vector A_i as a self-router—is conceptually clean, and the associative-memory framing (keys = rows of A, values = columns of B) is a coherent and intuitive way to motivate rank-level gating.

The empirical evaluation is broad: CLIP (X-TAIL, MTIL) with Transfer/Average/Last metrics, T5-large across 3 and 15-task orderings, LLaMA2-7B, and a fine-tuning/forgetting study with Llama-3.1-8B on CodeAlpaca vs. HumanEval/MMLU. Reporting mean±std over 3 runs (Table 13) is a positive practice.

MoRA shows consistent (if modest) improvements over strong baselines such as CoDyRA, RAIL-Primal, MoE-Adapter, and LB-CL across nearly all reported metrics, and the self-activation design removes the extra router parameters (Table 10/15), yielding a favorable parameter/activated-parameter budget.

Reproducibility information is reasonably complete: architectures, ranks, learning rates, batch sizes, temperatures, thresholds, task orderings, and datasets are specified, with code promised on acceptance.
weaknesses: The headline claim—that self-activation beats a learned router—is not supported by the paper's own ablation. In Table 4, Self-activation (65.94 Avg / 69.85 Last) is essentially tied with Non-self-activation (65.97 / 69.76) and is clearly *below* MoE-LoRA (69.45 / 74.53). The large gains only appear once sharpness control τ is added (71.15 / 79.62). Thus the narrative that rank-level self-routing is the key innovation is overstated; the dominant contributor appears to be temperature scaling, and the full MoRA result is a combination whose parts are not cleanly isolated.

Gains over the closest prior art are small and sometimes within noise on individual domains. X-TAIL Average: 72.7 vs. CoDyRA 71.3; MTIL Average: 73.9 vs. 73.3; LM Table 8: 69.72 vs. LB-CL 69.2. Several per-dataset gaps (e.g., X-TAIL Transfer 63.3 vs. 63.2) are negligible, weakening the significance claim.

Originality is incremental. Mixtures of low-rank subspaces for LoRA (e.g., MoS, Wu et al. 2024a) and rank-selective continual LoRA (CoDyRA) are closely related, yet MoS is not compared and the differentiation from CoDyRA is compressed to one sentence. The associative-memory reading of W and ΔW is borrowed from prior work (Meng et al. 2022; Geva et al.) rather than new.

The three motivating 'challenges' (interference, redundancy, routing ambiguity) are asserted rather than measured. No experiment directly quantifies cross-expert interference, redundancy, or router instability, so the motivation remains rhetorical.

Presentation quality is weak. The abstract is garbled (the 'However, this design introduces three key challenges' sentence has no clear antecedent), and the bibliography contains numerous malformed/incorrect entries (e.g., 'Grattafori et al.', 'Li & Hosem 2017', 'Douvitskiy', and several entries with corrupted author lists), which impedes verification of baselines and citations.

A potential training pathology is unexamined: TopK masking assigns -inf to non-selected ranks, so unselected ranks receive no gradient during training. The paper does not analyze how newly initialized ranks ever enter the top-k, nor whether dead/dormant ranks accumulate—an issue that is especially important in the incremental 'add r ranks per task' regime.

The forgetting/generalization analysis (Table 2) rests on a single model and a single fine-tuning dataset (Llama-3.1-8B on CodeAlpaca), and the reported MMLU gain over the base model is tiny (63.70 vs. 63.45), so the generalization claim is thinly evidenced.

strengths: Elegant and well-motivated method: decomposing each rank-r LoRA update into r rank-one components and treating each as an independent expert, grounded in the key-value associative-memory interpretation. This yields fine-grained experts without a separate router, since the key A_i naturally serves as a router for its value B_i, saving parameters and reducing routing confusion.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three distinct regimes: vision-language CL (X-TAIL and MTIL with CLIP), language-model CL (T5-large, LLaMA2-7B, standard and 15-task sequences), and general fine-tuning/forgetting analysis (Llama3.1-8B on CodeAlpaca with HumanEval and MMLU), with multiple task orderings and standard Transfer/Average/Last metrics.

Consistent and sometimes substantial gains: MoRA attains state-of-the-art results on X-TAIL (Avg 72.7 vs CoDyRA 71.3), MTIL (73.9), T5-large CL (77.6 avg vs LB-CL 76.7), and long 15-task sequences, while improving out-of-domain generalization and reducing forgetting on MMLU subjects.

Strong parameter efficiency: MoRA reaches HumanEval performance comparable to a rank-32 LoRA using roughly one-third of the activated parameters (26.2M activated / 41.9M trained), and Table 10 shows per-task trainable parameters at most equal to standard LoRA.

Thorough ablations isolating each component (mixture strategy, top-k rank selection, sharpness control, test-time thresholding) plus activation-budget and temperature/threshold sweeps, and a robustness study (Table 13) reporting mean±std over three runs with lower variance than baselines.

Interpretable visualization analysis (Figs. 3, 5, 6) supporting the claims of rank specialization, knowledge reuse across tasks, and forgetting mitigation, along with statistical analyses (Figs. 7–9) showing that <10% of ranks capture 99% of activation mass.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters (rank, budget, temperature, threshold, optimizer, iterations), dataset and prompt descriptions, an LLM-usage disclosure, and a commitment to release code.
weaknesses: The central 'self-activation' claim is only weakly supported by the ablations. In Table 4, self-activation alone (Transfer 60.26 / Avg 65.94 / Last 69.85) is essentially indistinguishable from a learned rank-level router (Non-self-activation: 60.09 / 65.97 / 69.76) and actually underperforms plain MoE-LoRA (62.56 / 69.45 / 74.53); the large gains only appear once temperature/sharpness control is added (62.07 / 71.15 / 79.62). This suggests the headline benefit comes from the combination of fine granularity plus sharpness tuning, not from self-activation per se, which the paper does not reconcile.

Improvements over the strongest baselines are often marginal: X-TAIL Transfer 63.3 vs CoDyRA 63.2, Last 80.9 vs 79.2, MTIL 73.9 vs CoDyRA 73.3, and MTIL Transfer 69.7 vs 69.9 (a loss). Statistical significance is only established for one setting (Table 13), so the robustness of the reported margins across all benchmarks is not fully demonstrated.

The method introduces several sensitive hyperparameters (activation budget k, temperature τ_MoRA, test-time threshold δ), and the appendix notes the optimal temperature varies across architectures (τ=0.1 for T5/CLIP vs 0.5 for Llama3.1-8B). This raises concerns about tuning burden and cross-architecture robustness that are not systematically analyzed.

The parameter-efficiency narrative is nuanced: on the CodeAlpaca experiment MoRA still trains 41.9M parameters (matching rank-32 LoRA) and only the activated count (26.2M) is reduced. The distinction between trained and activated parameters should be stated more carefully, and the claim of 'roughly one-third of the activated parameters' relies on a single comparison.

The rank activation budget k is fixed per benchmark (16 for CLIP, 4 for LM) and grows with the number of accumulated ranks; the paper does not analyze behavior as ranks accumulate over very long task streams or the risk of rank explosion in the absence of pruning at scale.

There is no dedicated limitations section. Potential failure modes (e.g., when relevance signals from A_i are weak, or when many tasks share overlapping subspaces and gating collapses) are not discussed, and the generalization claim rests largely on a single fine-tuning experiment.

strengths: Well-motivated and coherent framework: the progression from LoRA → MoE-LoRA → MoRAM is clearly argued, and grounding the method in the linear-associative-memory view (Kohonen/Anderson) gives a principled lens for treating rank-1 components as atomic key–value memory units.

The self-activation mechanism that eliminates the external router is a genuinely useful design choice: it directly targets the documented routing-collapse failure mode in MoE-LoRA and adds no extra routing parameters, while enabling content-addressable retrieval that scales with the memory bank.

The anti-forgetting results on TRACE are the strongest evidence in the paper: BWT is reduced to 1.37 (LLaMA-2-7B-Chat) vs 3.46 for TreeLoRA and to 2.74 (Gemma-2B-it) vs 8.50, which is a substantial, consistent improvement over competitive baselines with small standard deviations over three runs.

The ablation in Table 4 is honest and informative: it explicitly shows that self-activation alone (60.26/65.94/69.85) underperforms the coarse MoE-LoRA baseline (62.56/69.45/74.53), and that top-k, temperature, and threshold each contribute to the final result. This transparency strengthens confidence in the component design.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: detailed hyperparameters (rank, k, τ, δ, learning rates, epochs, hardware) are provided for each benchmark, and key experiments (TRACE, robustness, InfLoRA comparison) report mean ± std over multiple runs.

The qualitative visualizations (Figs. 3, 6, 7) effectively support the two claimed properties—rank specialization and knowledge reuse across tasks—and the aggregated activation heatmap (Fig. 5) corroborates the per-example patterns statistically.

The CodeAlpaca experiment (Table 3) provides useful evidence that the atomic decomposition preserves out-of-domain generalization (e.g., Logic 48.41 vs 42.85 for rank-32 LoRA) while activating roughly one-third of the parameters, and the trade-off is well framed.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of "significantly outperforming state-of-the-art" is not well supported on the CLIP benchmarks. On X-TAIL (Table 1), MoRAM is only ~1.7 points above CoDyRA on Last (80.9 vs 79.2) and ~1.4 on Average (72.7 vs 71.3), and essentially ties on Transfer (63.3 vs 63.2); on MTIL (Table 12) the margin is ~1.3 points. No error bars are reported for Table 1, so statistical significance is unclear and the language overstates the evidence.

Novelty is incremental rather than foundational. The associative-memory interpretation of weight matrices, the decomposition of LoRA into rank-1 components, and cosine-similarity-based gating all have antecedents; the main new element is the specific combination of rank-1 atoms with intrinsic-key routing. The paper does not sufficiently position these individual ingredients against the closest prior art.

There is an unresolved conceptual tension in the self-activation design: the key vectors A are simultaneously the routing signal and the representation. The paper acknowledges that imposing regularization on the routing "improperly hinders the learning of the key vectors," but it never justifies theoretically why optimizing keys for representation yields reliable retrieval keys, nor why specialization emerges without load-balancing; this is asserted empirically rather than explained.

The parameter accounting is confusing and potentially misleading. Table 11 lists MoRAM as "rd_in + kd_out" trainable parameters, but all r value vectors are stored and receive gradients across the training stream (only the forward compute is reduced by k). The claim that the trainable count is "at most the same as a standard LoRA" conflates storage, training, and active-compute costs and needs clarification.

The inference-time threshold selection (Eq. 8) and its interaction with top-k masking are ad hoc and under-analyzed. Fig. 4b shows that the temperature τ strongly controls the plasticity/stability balance (high τ surpasses SOTA on transfer), yet a moderate value is chosen without a principled criterion, and the same concern applies to δ.

The claimed sub-linear memory expansion via pruning is only lightly evaluated: a single top-99%-activation-mass criterion yielding ~30% pruning is reported, which is not enough to substantiate the scalability claim, especially given the stated linear storage growth.

On individual X-TAIL domains the method does not dominate (e.g., Food 84.4 vs CoDyRA 84.6, Flowers 83.9 vs 83.4), which is consistent with the gains being within noise and weakens the broad superiority narrative.

strengths: Interesting and coherent conceptual framing that connects the rank-r LoRA update to a linear associative memory view (each rank-1 component as an atomic key-value pair), and uses this to motivate a self-activation routing scheme that removes the external router in MoE-LoRA.

Broad empirical coverage: CLIP (X-TAIL and 5-shot MTIL), LLMs on TRACE with three backbones, standard and 15-task LM CL benchmarks, SuperNI, and code generation, plus ablations and rank-activation analyses.
Reproducibility is reasonably strong: detailed hyperparameters, task orders, prompts, metrics, and per-task parameter/GPU-memory accounting are provided in the appendix.

The backward-transfer (forgetting) improvements on TRACE are meaningful (e.g., BWT 1.37 vs 3.46 for TreeLoRA on LLaMA-2), and the replay-free SuperNI result (AP 39.62 vs 26.37 for O-LoRA) is a genuinely large gap.
The incremental rank-1 expansion with freezing of old atoms is a clean, implementable design, and the post-pruning analysis shows the learned representation is sparse.
weaknesses: Central claims are not well supported by the magnitudes reported. On most benchmarks the gains are marginal or within noise: X-TAIL Average 72.7 vs CoDyRA 71.3, MTIL 73.9 vs 73.3, standard CL 77.6 vs LB-CL 76.7, 15-task 69.72 vs 69.2, and Transfer on X-TAIL 63.3 vs 63.2. This contradicts the repeated 'significantly outperforms' framing.

The code-generation experiment (Table 3) undercuts the generalization claim: MoRAM matches LoRA (r=32) exactly on HumanEval (47.56) and is essentially tied on MMLU (63.70 vs 63.59), so the 'superior out-of-domain accuracy' claim rests on small per-subject differences and a parameter-count argument rather than a clear capability gain.

Hyperparameter inconsistency: the main text states the selected temperature is τ_MoRAM = 0.01 (Sec. 4.3), while Appendix A.1 states τ = 0.1 for CLIP and 0.03 for TRACE. This is a concrete reproducibility/consistency problem.

The ablation in Table 4 is confusing and arguably undermines the mechanism: self-activated retrieval alone (Average 65.94) and with sparsity (66.52) are worse than the coarse MoE-LoRA baseline (69.45); only the full combination reaches 72.70. This suggests the components are individually fragile rather than that the proposed retrieval is inherently superior.

Novelty is moderate and somewhat overstated. The associative-memory view of weights is borrowed (Kohonen 1972; Anderson 1972), and 'self-activation' is effectively a linear router whose weights are the LoRA A rows—i.e., a constrained router rather than an elimination of routing. The distinction from a learned router is not rigorously argued.
The 'sub-linear expansion' claim is not substantiated: pruning retains the top 99% activation mass and removes only ~30% of storage, which is still linear growth in the number of tasks.

Presentation problems: garbled/duplicated table headers (e.g., the TRACE header 'FIS/ICL)', the corrupted Table 19), low-resolution figures, and dense cross-referencing make several key results hard to verify.

No direct analysis is provided on whether the self-activation scores actually correspond to semantically meaningful 'keys', or whether the observed specialization (Fig. 3) is an artifact of the sharpened softmax rather than the associative-memory design.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework: reframes LoRA updates as atomic rank-1 key-value associative memories, enabling fine-grained expert specialization and input-dependent retrieval.
Eliminates the external router by tying routing weights to the key vectors (A_i x), reducing extra parameters and potentially mitigating router collapse; the mechanism is simple and elegant.
Extensive experiments across CLIP (X-TAIL/MTIL), LLMs (TRACE), language classification, SuperNI, and code fine-tuning, with many baselines and detailed appendix results.
Strong results on backward transfer (BWT) in TRACE and improved stability/forgetting mitigation, often with fewer active parameters (e.g., Table 3, Table 16).
Ablation and visualizations provide insight into rank specialization, knowledge reuse, and forgetting reduction; post-pruning analysis shows storage can be reduced with minimal performance loss.
Reproducibility details are mostly provided in the appendix: datasets, optimization settings, hyperparameters, and compute infrastructure.
Impact statement thoughtfully addresses potential misuse and mitigation strategies.
weaknesses: Central mechanism attribution is not fully supported. In Table 4, self-activated retrieval alone (avg 65.94, last 69.85) underperforms the coarse MoE-LoRA baseline (avg 69.45, last 74.53), and most of the full method's gain comes from temperature scaling (avg 71.15, last 79.62). A crucial control—temperature-scaled coarse MoE-LoRA or rank-1 with an external router plus temperature—is missing. This undermines the claim that fine-grained rank-1 experts and self-activation are the key to mitigating coarse-expert interference.

Main performance gains are modest on several benchmarks: X-TAIL average 72.7 vs CoDyRA 71.3; MTIL 73.9 vs 73.3; TRACE OP 44.54 vs TreeLoRA 43.52; language classification 77.6 vs LB-CL 76.7. Some improvements may be within noise, and statistical significance is not consistently reported across all main tables.

Hyperparameter inconsistency and sensitivity: Section 4.3 states a moderate τ_MoRAM of 0.01, while Appendix A.1 specifies τ_MoRAM=0.1 for CLIP. Temperature also varies across tasks/models (0.03, 0.1, 0.5). This raises reproducibility and tuning concerns, and no systematic sensitivity analysis is provided beyond limited plots.

Scalability and compute claims are not fully substantiated. Inference must score all accumulated rank-1 atoms, so per-token cost grows with the number of tasks; pruning is only post-hoc in Appendix A.10 and is not integrated into continual learning. The claimed 'sub-linear expansion rate' is not demonstrated in the main experiments.

Lack of an explicit limitations section. The paper does not discuss failure cases, when self-activation fails, load-balancing behavior beyond qualitative heatmaps, or the linear storage growth of the memory bank.

Missing comparisons to closely related LoRA mixture/subspace methods (e.g., MoSLoRA [87], MiLoRA [98]) and to a well-tuned generic MoE-LoRA with the same temperature scaling. The coarse MoE-LoRA baseline in Table 4 is not carried into the main benchmark tables.

The theoretical framing is mostly descriptive: Definition 1 is standard linear algebra, and there is no formal analysis of retrieval capacity, key normalization, or why self-activation should remain robust as the memory bank grows.
Presentation issues: typos ('avaliable', 'RAIL-Premal', 'Lave'), inconsistent table formatting, small figures, and ambiguous notation around thresholding on s_i versus w_i reduce clarity.
